cues.text:
Last time, we checked one agent's
proposals.

ARTF, the Agentic Real Time Framework,
lets hosts call specialist
services during an auction.

Now let's follow several specialists
working on the same OpenRTB request.

The SSP, the seller's platform, calls five
specialists together.

Each gets the starting envelope, which
wraps the auction data.
They share one deadline.

Parallel calls keep us from waiting for
each service in sequence.
Here's the request before and after.

Audience adds segments; curator adds deals
and raises the premium floor.

Those changes can affect which campaigns
consider the impression
and which bids qualify.
The host combines accepted proposals.
Metrics and quality add measurements.

Content ids describe the programme, while
audience segments describe viewer groups.

Each accepted write names its source
agent.

If a buyer receives unexpected data, we
can trace who proposed it.

What if two agents propose different
floors for the same deal?

This lab applies answers in configured
order, mostly to separate fields.
A production host needs a conflict policy.
Response speed shouldn't decide a price.

Now the request reaches two buyers, the
DSPs.

Each makes a bid and calls its own shader
through
GetMutations, ARTF's proposal interface.

Shading adjusts the offered price before
the bid returns to the exchange.

Alpha's shader and beta's shader sit on
separate internal networks.
The request agents sit with the seller.

In this lab, one shader has no direct
route to the other buyer.
The host controls that access.

Alpha's shaded bid falls below the deal
floor, so it's rejected.

Beta remains eligible and wins this
example.

A shader can change the price, but the
exchange still checks eligibility and
selects the highest eligible bid.
A deadline needs a fallback.

Here, a missing request agent's answer is
skipped; a failed shader
leaves the original bid.
These are lab policies.

If a service performs a required check,
continuing may be inappropriate.

This sample descriptor declares the
curator's image,
capabilities, and operating needs.
It helps explain deployment.

The envelope still limits the jobs offered
on each call.

Declaring a capability doesn't grant
unlimited auction access.

In this demo, ARTF's auction calls are
finished.

VAST now describes the ad and its
tracking.

We fetch dummy media and fire scripted
events.

Those requests don't prove a real viewer
watched the ad.
Let's repeat this path under load.

The driver requests twenty auctions a
second; monitoring shows
the rate actually achieved.

One auction can call several agents, so
auction rate and agent call
rate measure different things.

p95 estimates the time within which
ninety-five percent
of measured calls finish.

Read it with the auction path and buyer
call failures.

Fast typical calls don't tell us whether
every deadline was met.
Typed calls still need host checks.

Here we check call identity and offered
intents before combining proposals.

RTBlint checks our captured request
separately.

A deployed host still needs OpenRTB
validation before forwarding.

I'd start with one auction: follow a
proposal to the field the buyer receives.

Then test a missing answer and a
conflicting proposal.

ARTF supplies the shared interface; each
host remains
responsible for its decisions.
